title: Kim & Mauborgne / Blue Ocean Strategy, The Four Actions Framework
text:
## The Four Actions Framework

The Four Actions Framework is a core tool of blue ocean strategy developed by Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne. It poses four questions to challenge an industry's strategic logic and reconstruct buyer value elements so a company can create a new value curve. The four questions are:

## Eliminate

"Which factors that the industry takes for granted should be eliminated?" This forces managers to consider eliminating factors that companies in the industry have long competed on, even though these factors may no longer add value or may actually detract from it.

## Reduce

"Which factors should be reduced well below the industry's standard?" This prompts scrutiny of whether products or services have been over-designed in the race to match and beat competitors, raising cost structure with no gain.

## Raise

"Which factors should be raised well above the industry's standard?" This pushes discovery of compromises the industry forces customers to make.

## Create

"Which factors that the industry has never offered should be created?" This helps discover entirely new sources of value for buyers, create new demand, and shift the strategic pricing of the industry.

## Purpose and Value Innovation

The first two questions (eliminate and reduce) reveal how to lower cost structure versus competitors. The second two (raise and create) provide insight into how to lift buyer value and create new demand. Together they let a company break the trade-off between differentiation and low cost, creating a leap in value for buyers while keeping costs low. Cirque du Soleil and the wine brand written as [yellow tail] (Casella Wines) are cited as companies that reconstructed buyer value elements to offer buyers an entirely new experience while simultaneously keeping their cost structure low.

title: Kim & Mauborgne / Blue Ocean Strategy, The ERRC Grid
text:
## The ERRC Grid

The Eliminate-Reduce-Raise-Create (ERRC) Grid is an essential tool of blue ocean strategy developed by Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne. It is a simple matrix-like tool that drives companies to focus simultaneously on eliminating and reducing, as well as raising and creating, while unlocking a new blue ocean. It complements the Four Actions Framework by pushing companies to act on all four dimensions at once, producing a new strategic profile.

## The Four Categories

Eliminate: "Which factors that the industry has long competed on should be eliminated?" Reduce: "Which factors should be reduced well below the industry's standard?" Raise: "Which factors should be raised well above the industry's standard?" Create: "Which factors should be created that the industry has never offered?"

## Why It Works

The grid provides four immediate benefits: it enables the simultaneous pursuit of differentiation and low cost (breaking the value-cost trade-off); it immediately flags companies that are focused only on raising and creating, which lifts the cost structure and often over-engineers products and services; it is easily understood by managers at any level, driving high engagement in its application; and because completing the grid is a challenging task, it drives companies to robustly scrutinize every competing factor the industry takes for granted, revealing hidden assumptions. Case studies referenced include CitizenM hotels, the wine brand [yellow tail], Apple's iPhone, and Medellin's Metrocable.

title: Kim & Mauborgne / Blue Ocean Strategy, The Strategy Canvas
text:
## The Strategy Canvas

The Strategy Canvas is both a central diagnostic tool and an action framework for building a compelling blue ocean strategy. It is a one-page visual analytic that depicts the way an organization configures its offering to buyers in relation to those of its competitors.

## The Two Axes

The horizontal axis captures the range of factors that an industry competes on and invests in. This includes the product, service, and delivery factors where competitors typically concentrate their efforts. The vertical axis represents the offering level that buyers receive across all of these key competing factors, showing what customers actually experience from each competitor's strategic approach.

## The Value Curve

A value curve, also called a strategic profile, is the graphic depiction of a company's relative performance across its industry's factors of competition. It visually shows how each player compares on the identified competitive factors. When rivals' value curves converge and look alike, it is a signal of red ocean competition on the same factors.

## Dual Purpose

The tool serves two functions. First, current state analysis: it reveals the competitive factors, the level of offering buyers receive, and the existing strategic profiles, exposing how the strategies of the major players look to customers. Second, future orientation: it shifts strategic focus from competitors to alternatives and from customers to noncustomers, enabling a company to visualize blue ocean strategic moves that break from red ocean competition. A compelling blue ocean value curve has focus, divergence from rivals, and a compelling tagline.

title: Michael Porter / Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness (HBS), The Five Forces
text:
## Porter's Five Forces

The Five Forces is a framework for understanding the competitive forces at work in an industry, and which drive the way economic value is divided among industry actors. It was first introduced by Michael Porter in 1979. The framework helps a company assess industry attractiveness and its competitive positioning.

## Threat of New Entrants

New competitors can force current players to keep prices down and spend more to retain customers. Entry barriers include economies of scale, the cost of building brand awareness, access to distribution channels, and government restrictions. The threat level depends on the capabilities of potential entrants.

## Bargaining Power of Suppliers

Powerful suppliers can use their negotiating leverage to charge higher prices or demand more favorable terms from industry competitors. Supplier power increases when few suppliers exist for an essential input or when switching costs are high.

## Bargaining Power of Buyers

Powerful customers can use their clout to force prices down or demand more service at existing prices. Buyer power is strongest when customers are large relative to competitors, when products lack differentiation, and when switching costs are low.

## Threat of Substitute Products or Services

Substitutes meet the same underlying need that the industry's product meets in a different way. The threat intensifies when substitutes offer attractive pricing and switching costs remain low.

## Rivalry Among Existing Competitors

Intense rivalry drives down prices or dissipates profits by raising the cost of competing. Rivalry is most damaging when competitors are numerous, industry growth is slow, or exit barriers are high.

## Impact on Profitability

The Five Forces determine the competitive structure of an industry and its profitability. Industry structure, combined with a company's relative position within the industry, fundamentally drives profitability. The framework helps companies anticipate shifts in competition, shape how industry structure evolves, and find better strategic positions. A critical implication is that industry structure, not whether an industry is high-tech or low-tech, growing or mature, is the more durable determinant of average industry profitability.

title: Michael Porter / Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness (HBS), The Value Chain
text:
## The Value Chain

The value chain is a powerful tool for disaggregating a company into its strategically relevant activities in order to focus on the sources of competitive advantage. It breaks down operations to identify which specific activities drive higher prices or lower costs. The activities, and the overall value chain in which activities are embedded, are the basic units of competitive advantage.

## The Larger Value System

A company's value chain is typically part of a larger value system that includes companies either upstream (suppliers) or downstream (distribution channels), or both. This broader perspective requires managers to view each activity as contributing value incrementally to the final product or service, rather than merely as a cost center. Porter distinguishes primary activities (such as inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, marketing and sales, and service) from support activities (such as firm infrastructure, human resource management, technology development, and procurement); margin is the difference between total value delivered and the collective cost of performing the activities.

## Strategy and the Activity System

Strategy is reflected in the set of choices about how the activities in the value chain are configured and linked together. Success depends not just on executing individual activities well, but on how they interconnect systematically. Integrating best practices matters, but doing things effectively is not the same as doing things differently, which is the crucial distinction between operational excellence and strategic differentiation.

title: Michael Porter / Institute for Strategy and Competitiveness (HBS), Creating a Successful Strategy
text:
## Competitive Strategy Is About Being Different

Competitive strategy is about being different. It means deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value. A company can outperform rivals only if it can establish a difference that it can preserve.

## The Five Essential Elements of a Sound Strategy

First, a unique value proposition compared to competitors, setting the company apart in the marketplace. Second, a distinctive value chain: determining how the organization will operate differently to deliver on its value proposition. Third, strategic trade-offs: making deliberate decisions about what not to do, establishing clear boundaries around business activities. Trade-offs are the choices that make a position sustainable because they impose limits on what a company will offer and make it costly for rivals to imitate. Fourth, fit across the value chain: ensuring that activity choices fit together and reinforce each other throughout operations, so competitive advantage grows out of the entire system of activities rather than any single part. Fifth, continuity of strategic direction: maintaining continuity over time to sustain competitive advantage and to allow the organization and its customers to build deep capabilities and trust.

## Operational Effectiveness Is Not Strategy

Successful strategy requires more than operational improvements, it demands fundamentally different approaches. Companies like Southwest Airlines and IKEA rewrote the playbooks for their industries by choosing novel activity sets and establishing long-lasting, unique strategic positions. Operational effectiveness means performing similar activities better than rivals; strategic positioning means performing different activities from rivals, or performing similar activities in different ways.

title: Roger Martin, Decoding the Strategy Choice Cascade
text:
## The Strategy Choice Cascade

Roger Martin, co-author with A.G. Lafley of Playing to Win, defines strategy as an integrated set of five choices that cascade and reinforce one another. The five boxes, in a useful drafting order, are: Winning Aspiration (WA), the organization's overarching purpose and what winning looks like and for whom; Where-to-Play (WTP), the selection of markets, segments, geographies, channels, and customers where the company will compete; How-to-Win (HTW), the competitive approach that will let it win in those chosen places; Must-Have Capabilities (MHC), the distinctive set of activities and competencies required to win; and Enabling Management Systems (EMS), the systems, structures, and measures that build and sustain the capabilities.

## Where-to-Play and How-to-Win Are the Heart of Strategy

The combination of WTP and HTW is the heart of strategy, and they form an inseparable pair. A WTP choice is useless without a HTW for that WTP; likewise a HTW is useless without a WTP on which to focus. Neither can function independently, so they must be chosen and aligned together.

## Why All Five Boxes Matter

Strategy extends beyond the first three boxes. The last two, capabilities and management systems, provide a reality check by verifying whether the required capabilities can actually be built and sustained distinctively against competitors. Martin dismisses limiting strategy to vision or aspiration alone as delusional, and restricting it to only the first three boxes as lazy. Effective strategy requires all five elements working together iteratively through continuous refinement, testing and revising the choices until they form a coherent, mutually reinforcing system rather than a one-way sequence locked in top to bottom.

title: Richard Rumelt, Good Strategy Bad Strategy (summary of the book)
text:
## The Kernel of Good Strategy

Richard Rumelt argues that the core of good strategy, its kernel, has three elements: a diagnosis, a guiding policy, and a set of coherent actions. Diagnosis: a great deal of strategy work is trying to figure out what is going on. It comprehends the situation, defines the nature of the challenge, and identifies the critical obstacles to progress, separating the truly important aspects from the mass of detail. Guiding policy: the overall approach chosen to cope with or overcome the obstacles identified in the diagnosis. Like the guardrails on a highway, the guiding policy directs and constrains action without fully defining it. Coherent action: the guiding policy must be translated into a set of coordinated and coherent actions, feasible steps that are consistent with one another and that actually carry out the policy. A hallmark of true expertise is coordinating actions so they reinforce rather than fight one another.

## The Four Hallmarks of Bad Strategy

Rumelt identifies four hallmarks that reveal bad strategy. First, fluff: a form of gibberish masquerading as strategic concepts, using inflated words and abstruse jargon to create the illusion of high-level thinking rather than clarifying the situation. Second, failure to face the challenge: bad strategy fails to define or address the actual obstacle, so there is no way to evaluate or improve it. Third, mistaking goals for strategy: many bad strategies are just statements of desire (ambition, vision, values, or financial targets) rather than plans for overcoming obstacles. A good strategy honestly acknowledges the challenges being faced and provides an approach to overcoming them. Fourth, bad strategic objectives: objectives set by leaders that are a scrambled list of things to do (a dog's dinner) or that are blue-sky, restating desired outcomes without addressing how to reach them, and objectives that are just as difficult as the original challenge add no value.

## Proximate Objectives and Leverage

Good strategy sets a proximate objective, a target close enough at hand to be feasible: a proximate objective names a target that the organization can reasonably be expected to hit, even overwhelm. Good strategy also concentrates resources and action, applying strength against weakness through focus and leverage rather than spreading effort thinly across many goals.

title: Clayton Christensen Institute, Disruptive Innovation
text:
## Disruptive Innovation

Disruptive Innovation, a term coined by Clayton Christensen, describes a process by which a product or service takes root in simple applications at the bottom of the market, typically by being less expensive and more accessible, and then relentlessly moves upmarket, eventually displacing established competitors.

## Two Types of Disruptive Footholds

Low-end disruption: a cost-efficient business model enters an existing market's bottom segment. Because incumbents see this tier as unprofitable, they voluntarily cede the ground. An example given is CVS's MinuteClinic. New-market disruption: a company creates an entirely new consumer segment by offering simplified, more affordable versions of existing products, targeting previously underserved or nonconsuming populations, illustrated by smartphones taking on laptops.

## Why Incumbents Fail to Respond

Established firms rationally pursue sustaining innovations, incremental improvements that serve their most profitable customers, and so they voluntarily move upmarket and cede lower tiers. In steel, integrated mills earned only about 7 percent margins on rebar versus mini-mills' 20 percent or more, making it financially sensible for the incumbents to abandon the low-margin business rather than invest to defend it against the disruptive technology. Incumbents become trapped by their existing business model, unable to operate the new approach at the necessary scale while protecting legacy operations.

## Disruptive vs Sustaining Innovation

Sustaining innovations improve existing products for current customers along the dimensions they already value, commanding premium prices; incumbents almost always win the sustaining battle. Disruptive innovations deliberately sacrifice performance on traditional measures at first, prioritizing accessibility, simplicity, and affordability to reach nonconsumers or overserved populations, then improve over time until they meet mainstream needs and displace the incumbents. A key caution: disruption is a process, not a product, and not every novel or breakthrough innovation is disruptive in this specific technical sense.

title: Osterwalder & Pigneur / Wikipedia, The Business Model Canvas (nine building blocks)
text:
## The Business Model Canvas

The Business Model Canvas, developed by Alexander Osterwalder and Yves Pigneur in Business Model Generation, is a strategic management template that describes a business model through nine building blocks grouped into infrastructure, offering, customers, and finances.

## Infrastructure

Key Activities: the most important activities in executing a company's value proposition, for example creating an efficient supply chain. Key Resources: the resources necessary to create value for the customer, considered assets needed to sustain and support the business, spanning human, financial, physical, and intellectual resources. Key Partnerships (partner network): buyer to supplier relationships and alliances a company cultivates to optimize operations, reduce risk, and focus on its core activities.

## Offering

Value Propositions: the collection of products and services a business offers to meet the needs of its customers, distinguishing it from competitors through elements such as newness, performance, customization, design, brand, price, cost reduction, risk reduction, accessibility, or convenience.

## Customers

Customer Segments: the different groups of people or organizations a business aims to reach and serve, identified by distinct needs and attributes (mass market, niche market, segmented, diversified, or multi-sided platforms). Channels: the ways a company delivers its value proposition to customers, through direct channels, partner channels, or both. Customer Relationships: the types of relationships established with each customer segment, ranging from personal assistance to self-service to co-creation.

## Finances

Cost Structure: the most important monetary consequences of operating under a given business model, including fixed costs, variable costs, and economies of scale or scope. Revenue Streams: the way a company generates income from each customer segment, through asset sales, usage fees, subscription fees, lending or leasing, licensing, brokerage fees, or advertising.

title: Bruce Henderson / Corporate Finance Institute, BCG Growth-Share Matrix
text:
## The BCG Growth-Share Matrix

The Boston Consulting Group Matrix, created by Bruce Henderson of BCG, is a business planning tool used to evaluate the strategic position of a firm's brand or product portfolio. It is a two-by-two classification that plots each business unit on two axes. The horizontal (X) axis is relative market share, a measure of competitive strength. The vertical (Y) axis is market growth rate, an indicator of expansion potential, with roughly 10 percent typically distinguishing high growth from low growth.

## The Four Quadrants

Question Marks: high growth, low market share. These are the most managerially intensive products and require heavy investment; the goal is to turn them into Stars, otherwise they decline into Dogs. Stars: high growth, high market share. Market leaders that demand significant investment to retain their position, generating substantial cash flow and eventually migrating to Cash Cows as their market matures. Cash Cows: low growth, high market share. Established leaders requiring minimal investment that generate high cash used to fund Stars and Question Marks. Dogs: low growth, low market share. Self-sustaining but stagnant units that generate little cash and are typically divested or phased out unless they serve a complementary role.

## The Cash-Flow Logic

The framework assumes that increased relative market share results in increased cash flow through economies of scale and the experience curve. The strategic implication is to milk Cash Cows and redeploy their cash into Stars and selected Question Marks, while divesting Dogs, so the portfolio stays balanced over time. A known criticism is that the model treats market share and growth as the only drivers of profitability and ignores synergies between units and other sources of advantage.

title: Hamilton Helmer, 7 Powers: The Foundations of Business Strategy (faithful book summary)
text:
## Power: Benefit and Barrier

Hamilton Helmer defines Power as the set of conditions creating the potential for persistent differential returns. Every Power must combine two elements at once. The Benefit: the conditions must materially augment cash flow, through higher prices, reduced costs, or lessened investment needs. The Barrier: the benefit must persist, preventing competitors from arbitraging the advantage away. Strategy, in Helmer's view, is the study of the fundamental determinants of potential business value, and Power is what makes value durable.

## The Seven Powers

Scale Economies: benefit is reduced unit cost as business size grows; barrier is prohibitive costs of share gains for a challenger who would have to match your scale. Network Economies: benefit is that the value of the service to each customer increases as new customers join; barrier is the winner-take-all dynamic where advantage compounds with scale. Counter-Positioning: a newcomer adopts a new, superior business model that the incumbent does not mimic because of anticipated collateral damage to its existing business; the barrier is precisely that collateral damage. Switching Costs: a customer values compatibility across repeated purchases from one firm; benefit is the ability to charge a premium on follow-on sales; barrier is that rivals must compensate customers for the cost of switching. Branding: an asset that communicates information and evokes positive emotions, raising willingness to pay; benefit is higher pricing through affective valence or uncertainty reduction; barrier is that a brand can only be built over a lengthy period. Cornered Resource: preferential access at attractive terms to a coveted asset that independently enhances value; barrier is fiat, protection by decree or loyalty rather than ongoing market competition. Process Power: operational excellence embedded in the organization plus hysteresis; benefit is sustained product improvement and cost reduction; barrier is hysteresis, the advances are hard to replicate because they are complex and opaque.

## Power Over Time

The origination of each Power is tied to a phase of the business. Scale economies, network economies, and switching costs are typically established during the rapid growth phase when compelling value is first attained, while branding and process power become more attainable after growth slows.

title: Michael Porter / Wikipedia, Porter's Generic Strategies and Stuck in the Middle
text:
## Porter's Three Generic Strategies

Michael Porter argued that a firm's strengths ultimately fall into one of two headings, cost advantage or differentiation, and applying these across a broad or narrow competitive scope yields three generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation, and focus.

## Cost Leadership

A cost leadership strategy competes by achieving lower cost than its rivals across a broad market, sustaining profitability through economies of scale, standardized products, efficient operations, and tight cost control. The cost leader can then either charge industry-average prices to earn above-average returns or price below rivals to gain share.

## Differentiation

A differentiation strategy distinguishes offerings through unique attributes valued by customers, such as superior quality, design, technology, or brand, allowing the firm to command a higher price. Examples cited include Apple's design capabilities and Nike's brand positioning. The premium must exceed the extra cost of being unique.

## Focus

A focus strategy targets a narrow segment rather than the broad market and comes in two variants: cost focus (offering the lowest price to a niche) and differentiation focus (emphasizing uniqueness within a niche). The focuser wins by serving its narrow target better than broad-line competitors can.

## Stuck in the Middle (the classic anti-pattern)

Porter emphasized that a firm that tries to pursue more than one generic strategy at once, for example combining cost leadership with differentiation, risks losing the entire focus of the organization because these approaches require conflicting operational priorities and cultures. A firm that fails to make a clear strategic choice becomes stuck in the middle and typically underperforms competitors who are committed to a single generic strategy. Being stuck in the middle usually means below-average profitability, because the cost leader, the differentiators, and the focusers are all better positioned to compete in any segment.

title: Igor Ansoff / Wikipedia, The Ansoff Matrix (Product-Market Growth)
text:
## The Ansoff Matrix

The Ansoff Matrix, introduced by Igor Ansoff, is a product to market growth framework that helps a company decide its growth strategy. It uses two axes: products (existing or new) and markets (existing or new), producing four quadrants, each with a different growth strategy and risk level.

## Market Penetration

Grow by expanding sales of existing products within current markets, increasing market share through more aggressive promotion, competitive pricing, quality improvements, or winning competitors' customers. This is the lowest-risk quadrant because both product and market are known.

## Market Development

Take existing products into new markets, such as new geographies, new customer segments, or new channels (for example targeting industrial buyers instead of households, or expanding internationally). Risk is moderate because the products already have a proven track record.

## Product Development

Introduce new products to existing customers and markets, leveraging established brand reputation and customer loyalty, which requires R&D investment and integrating customer feedback. Risk is comparable to market development.

## Diversification

Launch new products into new markets at the same time, the riskiest quadrant because the firm lacks experience in both dimensions. Ansoff distinguished related diversification (concentric or horizontal, sharing some technology, market, or capability) from unrelated or conglomerate diversification (entirely different industries). Because it multiplies unknowns, diversification demands the strongest strategic rationale and the greatest caution.

title: Clayton Christensen Institute, Jobs to Be Done
text:
## Jobs to Be Done

Jobs to Be Done, developed by Clayton Christensen, holds that customers do not simply buy products, they hire them to make progress in specific circumstances. A job is the progress a customer is trying to make as they strive toward a goal or aspiration within particular circumstances. Just as people hire contractors to help them build houses or lawyers to build a case, people hire products or services when jobs arise in their lives, and they fire them when a better option comes along.

## Three Dimensions of a Job

Every job has three dimensions: functional (the practical task to be accomplished), social (how the customer wants to be perceived by others), and emotional (how the customer wants to feel). Understanding all three explains why customers make the choices they do far better than product attributes alone.

## The Milkshake Example

A fast-food chain studying milkshake sales found that customers hired the milkshake for different jobs at different times. In the morning, commuters hired it to make a boring drive more interesting and to stave off hunger, consumed one-handed in the car; in that job the real competition was not other milkshakes but bananas, bagels, and doughnuts. In the afternoon, parents hired the milkshake as a treat for their children, a completely different job with different competitors. Improving the product means improving it for the specific job, not for an average customer.

## Why It Beats Demographic Segmentation

Jobs Theory moves beyond market demographics and product attributes to expose the circumstance and the underlying motivation driving a choice. Two people in the same demographic can hire very different products for the same job, and the same person hires different products as the circumstance changes, so segmenting by the job to be done reveals real, actionable competition and unmet needs that demographic segmentation hides.

title: Baghai, Coley & White / Strategic Management Insight, McKinsey Three Horizons of Growth
text:
## The Three Horizons of Growth

The Three Horizons of Growth model originates from The Alchemy of Growth: Practical Insights for Building the Enduring Enterprise (1999) by Mehrdad Baghai, Steve Coley, and David White of McKinsey. It gives leaders a shared language and structure to manage a balanced growth portfolio, protecting current performance while systematically building the future, by developing several businesses in parallel regardless of their stage of maturity.

## Horizon 1: Core Business

Horizon 1 represents the established businesses that generate current profits and cash flow and by which customers and shareholders identify the company. The task is to shore up competitive positions and fully capture the remaining potential, while recognizing that these businesses eventually plateau and decline.

## Horizon 2: Emerging Businesses

Horizon 2 encompasses developing ventures with strong revenue potential in the near future that could potentially transform the organization. They require substantial investment, and significant profits may still be years away.

## Horizon 3: Future Seeds

Horizon 3 includes research projects, market tests, pilots, alliances, and minority stakes: the seeds of options that could yield future profitability if they succeed. They cost little today but preserve the right to play in tomorrow's markets.

## Managing All Three at Once

The central discipline is to manage all three horizons simultaneously and avoid the dangerous tendency to defer middle-term and long-term initiatives while over-focusing on the core. Timelines are deliberately flexible and depend on industry context; fast-evolving industries such as tech have shorter horizons, with Horizon 3 sometimes not stretching beyond a year or two.

title: Prahalad & Hamel / Wikipedia, Core Competency (The Core Competence of the Corporation, 1990)
text:
## Core Competency

C.K. Prahalad and Gary Hamel, in The Core Competence of the Corporation (Harvard Business Review, 1990), define core competencies as a harmonized combination of multiple resources and skills that distinguish a firm in the marketplace. They are the collective learning across the corporation, especially how to coordinate diverse production skills and integrate multiple streams of technology, and they are the true root source of competitive advantage.

## The Three Tests

A capability qualifies as a core competence only if it passes three tests. First, market access: it provides potential access to a wide variety of markets and can be leveraged to define new opportunities. Second, customer value: it makes a significant contribution to the perceived customer benefits of the end product. Third, difficult to imitate: it should be hard for competitors to copy, which makes the resulting advantage durable. Competitiveness derives from the ability to build, at lower cost and more speedily than competitors, the competencies that spawn unanticipated products.

## The Tree Metaphor

Prahalad and Hamel picture the diversified corporation as a tree. The root system that provides nourishment, sustenance, and stability is the set of core competencies. The trunk and major limbs are core products, the physical embodiments of the competencies. The smaller branches are business units, and the leaves, flowers, and fruit are the end products sold to customers. A company that judges rivals only by the fruit (end products) misses the strength of the roots. NEC, for example, leveraged core competencies in semiconductors, telecommunications, and consumer electronics to compete across many markets.

## Core Rigidities (the anti-pattern)

The flip side is that core competencies can harden into core rigidities: organizations become locked into past choices and yesterday's strengths and fail to adapt to new market demands, so a strength becomes a weakness when the environment shifts.

title: Wikipedia, PEST / PESTEL Analysis (macro-environmental scanning)
text:
## PEST and PESTEL Analysis

PEST analysis is a framework of external macro-environmental factors used in strategic management and market research. The base acronym stands for Political, Economic, Social, and Technological factors. Expanded variants add more letters: PESTLE (or PESTEL) adds Legal and Environmental; STEEPLE adds Ethical; and PMESII-PT is used in military contexts.

## The Factors

Political: government intervention in the economy, including tax policy, labour law, environmental law, trade restrictions, tariffs, and political stability. Economic: economic growth rates, currency and exchange-rate fluctuations, inflation, and interest rates. Social: cultural aspects, demographics and population growth, health and age distribution, career attitudes, and how social conditions affect demand for a company's products. Technological: research and development activity, automation, technology incentives, and the rate of technological change, which affect barriers to entry, make-or-buy decisions, and innovation. Legal: consumer protection, employment, health and safety, and antitrust or competition law. Environmental (ecological): climate, weather, and ecological impacts that matter for industries such as tourism, farming, and insurance.

## Role and Limitations

PEST is a scanning tool that maps the macro forces shaping an industry so they can feed into strategy, SWOT, and scenario work. Its main limitation is that it can help explain market changes in the past but is not always suitable to predict or foresee upcoming changes; it is a checklist of factors, not a strategy, and it does not by itself tell a firm what to do or where to compete.

title: Kim & Mauborgne / Blue Ocean Strategy, The Six Paths Framework
text:
## The Six Paths Framework

Kim and Mauborgne's Six Paths Framework identifies six conventional boundaries of competition that companies can look across to reconstruct market boundaries and discover blue ocean opportunities. Instead of accepting the industry's self-imposed assumptions, managers systematically look across each boundary.

## The Six Paths

Path 1, across alternative industries: rather than focusing only on rivals within its own industry, a company looks across the alternative industries that buyers weigh against it (alternatives serve the same purpose in a different form). Path 2, across strategic groups within an industry: instead of competing inside its own strategic group, a company examines across strategic groups, understanding why buyers trade up or down between them (for example, the factors that make buyers choose a luxury brand over an economy brand). Path 3, across the chain of buyers: rather than better serving the same buyer group, a company redefines the industry buyer group by shifting attention among purchasers, users, and influencers. Path 4, across complementary product and service offerings: instead of maximizing value within the bounds of its own product, a company looks across to the complementary products and services used before, during, and after its offering, solving for the total solution the buyer seeks. Path 5, across functional or emotional appeal: rather than improving price-performance within the industry's accepted functional or emotional orientation, a company rethinks that orientation and flips it (making a functional industry emotional, or stripping emotion out to make it functional and cheaper). Path 6, across time: instead of adapting to external trends as they occur, a company participates in shaping external trends over time, acting on a decisive trend early. The framework helps managers break away from conventional competition-based thinking and reconstruct where the market boundary should be.

title: Kim & Mauborgne / Blue Ocean Strategy, The Three Tiers of Noncustomers
text:
## The Three Tiers of Noncustomers

Kim and Mauborgne argue that to create a blue ocean and grow the market, a company should look not at existing customers but at noncustomers, the far larger ocean of untapped demand, and understand the commonalities across them rather than the differences among current customers. Noncustomers fall into three tiers by their distance from the industry.

## First Tier: Soon-to-Be Noncustomers

The first tier sits on the edge of the market. These are buyers who purchase the industry's offering minimally and out of necessity, but who are mentally noncustomers of the industry, ready to jump ship as soon as an alternative appears. Unlocking why they are waiting to leave reveals a large source of latent demand.

## Second Tier: Refusing Noncustomers

The second tier consists of people who have consciously considered the industry's current offering as an option to meet their needs but have deliberately decided against it, refusing to use it. Their refusal, once understood, points to what would bring them in.

## Third Tier: Unexplored Noncustomers

The third tier is the most distant: noncustomers in markets far removed from the industry who have never thought of the market's offerings as an option, because their needs and the associated business opportunities have always been assumed to belong to other markets.

## Strategic Application

The power of the framework lies in conversion. By focusing on the key commonalities across these three tiers of noncustomers and existing customers, rather than on finer segmentation of current buyers, a company can discover how to pull a mass of noncustomers into a new market, turning latent demand into real demand, which is the essence of blue ocean creation.

title: Kim & Mauborgne / Blue Ocean Strategy, The Buyer Utility Map
text:
## The Buyer Utility Map

The Buyer Utility Map, developed by Kim and Mauborgne, helps managers see an offering from the demand side and identify where an industry is failing to deliver value, so they can design exceptional utility rather than technology for its own sake. It maps two dimensions: the stages of the buyer experience and the utility levers that unlock value at each stage.

## Six Stages of the Buyer Experience Cycle

The buyer experience is a cycle of six stages, running more or less sequentially from purchase to disposal: purchase, delivery, use, supplements (complementary products and services needed to make the offering work), maintenance, and disposal. Each stage is a distinct part of the customer's journey where value can be added or destroyed.

## Six Utility Levers

Cutting across the stages of the buyer experience are the utility levers, the ways companies unlock utility for their customers: customer productivity, simplicity, convenience, risk reduction, fun and image, and environmental friendliness. The intersection of a stage and a lever is a utility space.

## Locating Blocks to Utility

By plotting where existing offerings sit on the thirty-six utility spaces (six stages by six levers), managers can see whether a new idea creates a genuinely different utility proposition, and crucially whether it removes the biggest blocks to utility that stand in the way of converting noncustomers into customers. Most incumbents cluster in the same few spaces (typically use and functional productivity), leaving whole stages and levers, and therefore whole blue ocean opportunities, untouched.

title: Kim & Mauborgne / Blue Ocean Strategy, Red Oceans vs Blue Oceans
text:
## Red Oceans vs Blue Oceans

Blue ocean strategy, developed by Chan Kim and Renee Mauborgne, is built on the contrast between two kinds of market space. Red oceans are all the industries in existence today, the known market space with defined boundaries and accepted rules of competition. In red oceans, companies try to outperform rivals to grab a greater share of existing demand; as the space gets crowded, products become commodities, competition turns cutthroat or bloody (hence red), and profits and growth are reduced.

## Blue Oceans

Blue oceans are all the industries not in existence today, the unknown market space, untainted by competition. In blue oceans, demand is created rather than fought over, and there is ample opportunity for growth that is both profitable and rapid. The aim is not to beat the competition but to make the competition irrelevant by creating a leap in value for buyers and the company, thereby opening up new and uncontested market space.

## Value Innovation, the Cornerstone

The cornerstone of blue ocean strategy is value innovation: the simultaneous pursuit of differentiation and low cost. Rather than accepting the conventional value-cost trade-off, where a firm must choose between higher value at higher cost or lower cost at lower value, value innovation breaks the trade-off by aligning the whole system of a company's activities toward achieving both. It places equal emphasis on value (for the buyer) and innovation; innovation without value tends to be technology-driven or futuristic, and value without innovation tends to be incremental. The research base behind the framework studied more than 150 strategic moves spanning more than 30 industries over 100 years.
